Coming from a constituency in which we have one of the largest penitentiaries, I have some matters I wish to bring before the Minister of Justice. I should like to urge once more that the warders and guards employed in the prisons should have at least a 44-hour week. Recently we have had quite a lot of people wanting a 40-hour week. This is a government institution, and surely we should not begrudge these men a 44-hour week. If, because of sickness or for any other reason, they have to work longer than that, such extra time should be allowed as overtime; or if that is against the regulations of the department, they should at least have time off equal to the extra time they put in. In case of sickness they may have to work a great many hours extra, so that I should like the minister to look into this matter and see if it is not possible to grant the penitentiary employees a 44-hour week.
On previous occasions I have appealed to the government in regard to the wages paid these men. I think they should receive more money because, if you want good men there, who will rehabilitate those who have gone wrong, you need a fine type of citizen, and with the wages you are paying to-day you will not get men of that type. The wages are not sufficient to attract men coming out of the armed forces. I refer to the report of the royal commission on the penal system of Canada, in which the commissioners had this to say:
It is also imperative that the pay of officers should be raised to a standard somewhat comparable to the rates prevailing in other similar services. It is hopeless to expect to get competent penitentiary officers at salaries that are considerably less than the wages paid to street cleaners in the large cities of Canada.
If there is anything we need to improve it is our penitentiaries, and that improvement can only be brought about by employing the best men available. So that I would ask the minister to take this into consideration.
Then I would suggest that when vacancies occur in the penitentiary service they be

advertised in all penitentiaries, so that men possessing the necessary qualifications may move from one part of the country to the other. This would mean more rapid promotion for good men and, I think, would be a step in the right direction. I also find that in this department as in others, when a man reaches the age of retirement and is entitled to three or six months' leave, another man cannot be employed until that leave is up. If you had a good man doing a good job before his service was completed, then you lose the benefit of that good work until he is replaced, and it means extra work for the remainder of the staff. I believe the civil service commission should make some recommendations to overcome that situation, In other departments you find that, when a man retires, somebody is ready to fill his place, and it should not be necessary to wait for six months before that is done.
Another matter I should like to mention is that ,the department is still working under the quota system, which means that a penitentiary where there is a small number of convicts is likely to be understaffed. I regard a penitentiary as something like the Queen Mary or the Queen Elizabeth. You would never think of sending either of these boats to sea without a full, adequate crew, but some penitentiaries in this country are being conducted with less than a full crew because the number of prisoners does not come up to the quota. I believe that should be changed, and the quota system should be abolished. Certain posts in a penitentiary have to be manned adequately at all times, and if you run short of crew you will run into difficulties right away; somebody is going to be neglected or someone is going to have too much to do.
I drew the minister's attention last year to the terrible housing ' conditions at Stony Mountain. They are disgraceful. The royal commission which investigated the penal system of Canada in 1936 said this:
Accommodation for the staff is inadequate. It is unreasonable and unnecessarily humiliating to ask members of the staff to live under conditions which now exist in officers' tenements belonging to the institution. These houses were built fifty years ago. They are without sanitary conveniences, and prisoners themselves are much more comfortably housed in their cells than officers in the penitentiary tenements.
Your commissioners are of the opinion that this state of affairs is destructive of the morale of the officers and that immediate steps should be taken to provide the staff and their families with respectable accommodation. In a large metropolitan centre the homes which are provided for the staff would, indeed, be condemned by the medical authorities.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: Since the hon. member for Broadview is in his seat I should like to deal with two or three of the points he raised at the opening of the debate on these estimates. The matter of the consolidation of the criminal code is being dealt with progressively by an important committee of the Canadian Bar Association, on which the attorneys general of all the provinces are represented and which, without cost to the federal treasury, is doing work which will be of considerable value to the Canadian public.
I understood the hon. member to say that when he commenced practice there were three county court judges in Toronto. I believe there are nine to-day functioning under His Honour Judge Parker. The county and district court judges are required by the constitution to be members of the bar; so that if there are any gentlemen administering justice who are not members of the bar they must be magistrates appointed by some other authority, because the British North America Act in sections 96 and 97 expressly requires that the judges of the county and district courts, as well as those of the superior court, shall be members of the bar.
There was a suggestion that the federal government should reimburse to the municipalities costs of the administration of justice. That would involve a substantial change in the distribution of powers and responsibilities between federal and provincial governments. Proposals for the reallocation of some of the responsibilities between the two authorities were submitted to the dominion-provincial conference, but unfortunately it was not possible to get an agreement on the proposals.
Until some reallocation is made, I am afraid we shall have to leave it to the provinces and municipalities to continue to bear the cost of performing services which under the constitution are their responsibility.
In bill No. 13, standing in the name of the hon. member, which he permitted to stand pending consideration of the estimates, suggestions are contained which would not be within the constitutional jurisdiction of this parliament. Parliament cannot say what laws will bind judges who preside over courts. It has no right to say that those judges will-respect judgments rendered by higher courts, except in criminal matters. But in all other matters the administration of justice is presided over by judges appointed by the federal authority. This parliament has, however, no right to say to them what judgments they will render, and by what authority they will feel they are bound.
The other bill standing in the name of the hon. member deals with responsibility for motorcar accidents. It was discussed when the hon. member was not in his seat, but I believe all hon. members appreciate the motives which prompted his making the suggestions contained therein. However, I believe there are some principles underlying the suggested changes which it would be dangerous to adopt. I do not believe it has been a principle in the criminal code that guilt will be presumed, or even that there would be guilt without the element of intent for which the code now provides. I should hope that with the provision of better vehicles-which will become possible as soon as they are available-for those large numbers who are anxious to get them, there will not be on the highways the kind of vehicles which were used during the war years, and that that will be one substantial means of diminishing the number of accidents occurring on the highways.
I do not think we can prevent accidents by having severe legislation in the criminal code, and I believe that on reconsideration the hon. member would not want the presumption of guilt, which his suggested changes contain, to become part of the administration of our penal law. The matter is one of concern to all of us. It is receiving consideration, and will be dealt with, if it is felt that there will be time at this session of parliament to give it the consideration it deserves.
As to the suggestions made by the hon. member for Selkirk, he knows that a commissioner of penitentiaries has been appointed. I have read more than once the report of the Archambault commission. There is very much that is good in it. There are certainly some
Sup-ply-Justice

assertions in it that are exaggerated. I have not had time myself to verify all the conditions described in that report, and it is because I did not have the time to do so myself that I wished to have a commissioner who would go about and see just exactly what the conditions are.
The hon. member says that there are houses at Stony Mountain that are fifty years old. I was born in a wooden house that was more than fifty years old when I was born, and whenever I have an opportunity to go back to it I find great comfort in it yet. So that age alone is not suificient to condemn a house. I said to the hon. member that there was a project for the construction of fifteen additional houses for the Stony Mountain penitentiary; but the hon. member knows that those who are living in the houses there, if they vacated them, would soon be replaced by others who have no houses at all. There is quite a serious housing shortage all over the country; and for the purposes of this year's budget every department was told to keep its construction down to the very minimum because the government did not want to be charged with taking material for its purposes when material was required so urgently for those who have no houses at all, and for whom provision has to be made first.
The money is available for the construction, but we are not prepared to regard as more urgent the requirements of ourselves and' of our civil service than the requirements of the rest of the population, especially of the returning veterans. That puts upon the replacing of those houses a time limit which is not within our control.
The hon. member asks, are we any nearer toward the completion than we were last December or November when the estimates were being considered last year? I hope we are. I hope we are getting nearer every day to a situation where building material will be easier and where some construction can be provided. We are certainly much nearer to it than we were a week ago when the forest operations in British Columbia were interrupted by the strike. If we can all of us get to work and keep at work and not do foolish things we shall get to an easier position much more quickly than if we continue to do some of the foolish things we have been doing during the last several months, and I hope we all realize that. We all have the same interest-labour and management, and management and labour -and I hope we shall all take the view of the *commissioner, I think he was, in New Zealand
'Mr. St. Laurent.]
who recommended to the people there that if we want to improve our conditions we must all get down and produce.

That is the only way to do it.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: To that extent we shall get nearer the time when there will be the fifteeen houses built around Stony Mountain penitentiary. The hon. member suggests the establishment of a bus service. My information is that there is a public bus service from Winnipeg to Stonewall along a highway that is within a couple of hundred yards of the administration building of the penitentiary. I have not been there myself. I have not been anywhere else since I came to Ottawa four and a half years ago. But recently a commissioner has been appointed who is going all around to see the situation for himself, and who was recommended to me as one who is practical in such matters, on whose reports I could rely, and who would have the tact to try to harmonize and coordinate the good will of all these organizations to which the hon. member for Davenport has referred with respect to prison after-care. That is a matter that is not within our jurisdiction. It is not to pass the buck that I say that. It is something which is deserving of the best efforts of all jurisdictions concerned.
One of the qualities that I was looking for in the appointee to the penitentiary commission was the fact that would make it possible for him to interview the authorities of the provinces and of the municipalities and try to promote coordination and cooperation between us. My experience has been that we make much more progress by conferences between officials than we do when members of the various governments are called together in conference. The extent to which there is in fact cooperation between the officers of the provincial governments and the officers of the federal government is much greater than what we were able to accomplish in the conferences that were held between the premiers of the provinces and the representatives of the dominion government. I think, after the commissioner of penitentiaries has had an opportunity of visiting not only the penitentiaries which are under our jurisdiction but the prisons which are under provincial jurisdiction, and seeing the men who are in charge of those institutions and discussing with them what can be done to improve the situation, we are apt to get better results than we got when the premiers of the provincial governments and the representatives of the federal government got together to discuss amendments to the constitution and transfers of jurisdictions and responsibilities.

In reply to the minister, I should like to tell him that about sixty years ago I was bom in a little house among the heather that had very poor conveniences, and I do not want to go back and live under the same conditions again. I do not want anybody else to live under those conditions. The conditions that were good enough fifty years ago are not good enough to-day.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am not saying that the house I was born in fifty years ago is in exactly the same condition to-day as it was then, and these houses around Stony Mountain penitentiary have been maintained and improved. I am not saying that they should not be replaced by something better as soon as it will be possible to get the materials to do so without taking that material away from those who need it to build homes for themselves. But the fact that a house is fifty years old does not in itself condemn it.

I agree with the minister to a certain extent, that an old house may be good. But if you want the best people to serve in Stony Mountain penitentiary you will not get them if they have to live in a house with no sanitary conveniences. You want the best people. The best people want something better than an outdoor toilet. The houses are fifty years old. I am ahead of the minister because I have been around there many times; I live not very far from there.
Careful.

Having reached the age of sixty years without going in, I think'I can keep out during the rest of my life.
I should like the minister just to touch on the matter of the hours of work. They are working there for less wages than they should be working for, and longer hours than they should be working.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am not prepared to admit that they are working more hours than they should work, or for less than they should be getting. I am prepared to admit that they are working forty-eight hours a week and that there is a feeling that men should not work forty-eight hours a week. I am not yet convinced that that is absolutely true, you know; but I am convinced that it will be necessary to have conditions there comparable with what conditions are elsewhere; and it was for the purpose of getting accurate, up-to-date information as to what should be done that the amendment to the Penitentiaries Act was made last year and that one penitentiary commissioner has been appointed. The fact of the matter is that whenever labour is at all "easy" we get a large number of applications for these penitentiary jobs. We do not always get them from the kind of people who should have the jobs. I agree with the hon. member that we should have improvement in our custodial staffs. It is something toward which we are working; and, from the reports I get about him, I have great confidence in the gentleman who has become the penitentiary commissioner, and who has already visited two of these institutions and made a thorough and careful investigation of the situation, who is proceeding to visit the others, and who will be able to make recommendations which can be implemented. When I had my conversation with him about the nature of his duties I told him that we wanted someone who would help us make in our penal system all the improvements that one could recommend to practical men as being things to be realized. I think we shall get somewhere; we have started in the right direction and we shall get results. But we shall not get at once a Borstal system controlled by a federal department, because that is something which would affect the whole of our penal institutions, and this government has control only of the penitentiaries, whilst there are certainly more than fifteen times as many institutions which are under provincial control. We have no actual jurisdiction over post-prison work. We have jurisdiction over these convicts while they are in the penitentiary, but as soon as they get out they are no longer within our jurisdiction. That does not mean that we should not take any interest in what happens; and it does not mean that we should not, with the Department of National Health and Welfare, endeavour to cooperate with the provinces and bring about, for instance, an application of the knowledge which has been acquired about mental hygiene. But that is not something which this house can deal with as its concern. We can be helpful, and we can endeavour to get the help of others, but we have not the jurisdiction to determine what is to be done in Canada about the matter. It is for that reason that I wanted someone who was recommended to me, who took all the "bugs" out of the military plans that were being prepared and had them workable before there were attempts made to implement them. I think that with that kind of advice we shall make real progress.

One further remark and I have finished. I am pleased that the minister has his commissioner appointed, and I hope I shall have the privilege of meeting him at Stony Mountain. I know that what I have said here to-night is true in every sense of the word, because I have visited this insti-

tution. The minister's deputy or assistant who spoke about going to Stonewall may not know that Stonewall is away in the other direction as far as the bus is concerned. The present government of Manitoba supplies a gaol bus and runs the warders to and from the provincial goal. The dominion government has far more money than the province; it should be able to do that too, until such time as material is available from the minister to build these new houses.

It is one of the cardinal principles of magna charta that the people shall take a large share in the administration of criminal justice. These institutions, whether rightly or wrongly managed, are managed by crown officers. I appreciate the difficulties which the minister and the officials of his department have in this connection, because, as the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe remarked, it is a work that does not bring much satisfaction; there is no occupation more open to criticism than that of those in charge, working all the time honestly, satisfying nobody.
There has been a marked increase in the criminal population. As members of the committee know, after every great war there is a great deal of trouble in dealing with this problem. Wars and rumours of wars and similar disturbances bring about a ' large increase in crime. The population of these penal institutions rose from 1,689 in 1919 to 3,803 at the last record, about the beginning of the war, and it is still going up by leaps and bounds.
There is an important public policy connected with this matter; so much so, that I wish to refer a few moments to-night to the inspection of these institutions. There is an act which relates to this matter; but the board of visitors, also the House of Commons and the Senate, might just as well be eliminated in this regard, because the method of inspection is a dead letter. Those confined in these institutions are forgotten. The public pay little or no attention to this problem.
I was chairman for seven years of a large police commission, and years ago, with Doctor Hastings, then the health officer, I visited one of the institutions in my own constituency of Broadview, the Toronto gaol. It was built not long after confederation. Doctor Hastings, then the health officer, and' I inspected it. Talk about any law of hygiene! Every known law of hygiene was violated. It is the same in all these institutions, federal, provincial and municipal, all over our province.
As I have said before, a federal prison commission was appointed in 1936. One of the

commissioners, Mr. Harry Anderson, who did much for prison reform, died shortly after his appointment. Visits by these commissioners were paid to every country in the world, and they brought in a report. The failure of the government of the day to introduce in Canada the Borstal system, which had such salutary results in the mother country some thirty years ago, has been criticized by all the synods and presbyteries in the country, by churches of all denominations, who have unanimously asked for some action. They look to this parliament for action. As I have said, the inspection is not what it should be. I appreciate the services of many of our officers. From our city we have as chief inspector, General Gibson, at the present time in Ottawa, a military man of sound judgment and good executive ability. But in my opinion the grand juries should be allowed to go once a year into these institutions that are under federal control, as they are allowed to inspect provincial penal institutions. When I was head of the police department in that city the grand jury in Hamilton on one occasion found three or four insane men in a certain institution. It is most important, in my opinion, that provision be made for inspection once a year of federal institutions by grand juries, as the late Chief Justice Meredith stated in the fall session some years ago in addressing the grand jury.
We might as well admit that we have no inspection worthy of the name. These institutions are inspected only by crown officers, and we might well inscribe over the door of everyone of these institutions the words that are found in Dante: "All hope abandon ye who enter here". I have spoken to some of the officers about the work done in these institutions, and I can find no reason why the report was not carried into effect. The war was pleaded as an excuse. I think the members of this house should take more interest in this question.
In the city of Toronto, away back in 1912, we established a gaol farm on Yonge street, North York, when we were going to close up the Toronto gaol, which was then a relic of the middle ages. The laws of public hygiene are unknown in many of these institutions. There are good officers and good men conducting that particular institution in Toronto, but they cannot properly handle all the work they have to do with the antiquated machinery at their disposal. There is one institution in Ottawa but it is in a favoured position. One of the evening papers in this city stated last fall that the $300,000 that is to be handed out to Ottawa as a subvention will be used to secure a new gaol and a new court house.

I should like to give the minister some constructive suggestions. Shortly before this house was called together there were a number of riots across Canada in. three institutions. The population in one of these institutions in Kingston and Collins Bay has increased considerably. A large number of military men have been brought back from Europe, some for minor offences, some for absence without leave and others for desertion, while there are thousands of others who have not yet been rounded up. I contend that under the present law they have no right to be housed in these institutions. They have been convicted of military offences, and the various wardens across Canada have no right under the present act to admit them. I suggest that they could bring action for damages in some cases in respect of such detention.
I wish to refer to another matter, and it is this. We are away behind the times in constitutional reform, in cabinet reform and in law reform. We have had no real law reform in this country. As a matter of fact, I have seen very little law reform since I was called to the bar a good many years ago. We are thirty years behind England. Little progress has been made in Canada in that direction in comparison with the mother country, where there is real reform. I suggest that one of the meanest acts ever passed was in connection with the imposition of "indeterminate sentences". In 1939 I introduced a bill dealing with this whole question. Provincial institutions could house convicted persons only for a year and three hundred and sixty-four days. That was the situation up to 1867 when these institutions were handed over to the government of Canada. I introduced my bill for the purpose of eliminating indeterminate sentences, which I contend are unfair. Indeterminate sentences were condemned severely by Mr. Justice Middleton, as will be found by reference to Ontario Law Reports of July, 1937, in the case of Rex versus Bond, at page 538. Why should a man be. kept indefinitely in prison, without hope of liberty, when he expects that in consequence of good conduct he may obtain his freedom? The fact is, however, that, under the indeterminate sentence, someone may come forward and report some conviction which the man had against him at some time or another, and the result is that the parole board turns down his application. The learned judge criticized the system in severe terms, and since that time it was also criticized) last year and the year before in the court of appeal of the province. He also referred to the Guelph 63260-174
institution. Various judges have condemned it in the strongest possible language and urged for a new institution for younger inmates.
All these law reports have been reported to the government, but nothing has been done about the matter. As I explained in introducing my bill in 1939, the Prisons and Reformatories Act gives the court jurisdiction to impose an indeterminate term in a reformatory. The bill proposes to substitute determinate for indeterminate sentences. The several expressions relating to "indeterminate sentence" are found in eighteen sections or subsections of the act, and the draftsman considers it inexpedient to amend each of such sections by a separate clause.
This bill would revert to the old law of sentences for a definite period only. The indeterminate legislation has definite period only. The indeterminate legislation has been condemned by many judges and magistrates as inhuman and illegal.
Canada's prisons at present are filled with youth, many first offenders, who have been unable to secure work. The lack of employment by cause and effect is one of the reasons for crime. Recently the appellate 'division of the supreme court of Ontario questioned the legality of such indeterminate legislation, since the provinces had only the right of providing confinement for one year and 364 days, and also condemned it on grounds of public policy. The law has not acted as a deterrent, nor is it reformative. It should be repealed, because in practice it confers on officials of these institutions the right to detain those who have not influence enough to have employment awaiting them at the end of a definite period, and gives to their decisions the force of statute law.
That state of affairs should not be tolerated and, as I have already stated, it was severely condemned. The government gave a list of inspectors three years ago. A great many of them have had a college education and all that kind of thing. In other words, they learn by experience; that is all. They know nothing about the work. Just fancy bringing in some outsider to become chief of a police force! At least they have to learn the business end of it. A representative from one of the large departmental stores came to see me some time ago. I said to him: "You cannot learn one department of your store in a day or two. How can you learn this business in a day?" This is one of the most important problems in the country. The report of the minister of March 31, 1945, shows that in the United States they have developed a programme of training young officers for this work, officers who have the

proper educational background. A great deal has been done in this regard. It is a most commendable thing. A few years ago the minister allowed the convicts to use the radio. That gave them some information from the outside world.
I believe that members of parliament should visit one or two of these institutions. A committee on legal law should be instituted in this house. They could make some visits and thereby strengthen the hands of the minister and his officers. I hope and trust that next year we shall not be pleading that the war prevented us from installing the Borstal system. As judges have pointed out, there is in Ontario no institution to which they can send an offender. I appreciate the good work that the minister and his officers have done, because he has a most difficult task. Anybody who has been a member of parliament for a few years must know that the hardest task in this house has been carried out by the Minister of Justice. He has given a great deal of time and thought to the matter, far more than any of us. I hope that something will be done, because I believe that this matter is one of the most important subjects with which we have to deal.

Perhaps some of our ideas in regard to the running of penal institutions in this country would be considered antiquated in other parts of the world. I should be interested to know from the minister the extent to which we have been appointing former military men to the top posts in penal institutions. I should like to register my opinion, for what it is worth, that the professional military type of mind should disqualify any man for the top position in any penitentiary. I say that with no desire to offend anyone. I do not believe, for instance, that the young men who volunteered to go overseas should be deprived of positions in our penitentiaries; but by the very nature of their inexperience and their youth they would not be taking these top positions to which I refer. I think it has been well established that military discipline is not what is required in dealing with people in these institutions, where the emphasis should be upon correction; that is to say, upon correction from the point of view of reform of character, rather than mere maintenance of iron discipline. I have noticed, as I expect other hon. members have, that sometimes those in charge of these institutions forget the object of them, forget the inmates and become buried in a mass of routine having to do with organization and administration, so that organization and administration become the thing and the inmates, whether of a school, a penal institution or what have you, are inclined to be forgotten.
